anchors.fact: A drink called the Cosmopolitan was already around San Francisco: a newspaper writer met it in 1987 as a Kamikaze with cranberry, and Cecchini remembers it as cheap vodka, bottled lime and grenadine (accounts differ). Most likely in 1988, at the Odeon in New York, he remade it: a lemon vodka new that year, the fresh lime and Cointreau the bar used in its Margaritas, and a little of the sweetened cranberry it kept for another drink.
anchors.meaning: He didn't invent something from nothing to be first. He fixed a thing he didn't think much of, for himself, with what was to hand.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me · soughtFor: Taste

anchors.fact: He made it as a staff drink, and was puzzled when customers started ordering it.
anchors.meaning: Going first is private before it's public. The Trend Setter isn't launching anything; they're just liking it.

anchors.fact: Other downtown bars began making it, "wrong and badly" in his words. By 1990 it was all over New York, and it became the one cocktail of its era that was a household name.
anchors.meaning: Once it's everyone's, it's usually done a bit worse. Said plainly, no bitterness.

anchors.fact: The young craft bartenders who came after rejected it (the flavoured vodka and the sweetened cranberry), and some bars wouldn't stock cranberry so they'd never have to make it. For years bartenders gave him grief for it and he'd say sorry. He shirked the credit, and in 2014 he said that five years earlier he'd have asked to be "unshackled" from it.
anchors.meaning: The real wound: not the crowd, but the people you respect rolling their eyes, and the pull to disown your own thing. Wanting out still lets them decide.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: The real me · soughtFor: Courage

anchors.fact: "That changed" (Simonson). As of 2026 (Lascelles, secondary) he still makes it at his own Long Island Bar in Brooklyn: 2:1:1:1, in a saucer coupe, with a lemon twist, and he likes it "shrill".
anchors.meaning: Take it back and make it your way, even now it's everyone's. Nothing on record says he ever stopped making it, and that's the point: he stopped letting others decide how he felt about it.
anchors.speaksTo: lens: My future self · texture: In control

anchors.fact: Three basil leaves, shaken with the drink and strained out. The *Flavor Matrix* gives basil as a surprise pairing for the berry family, cranberry included (pdf 52). The proportions stay his (2:1:1:1).
anchors.meaning: His spine, your mark. Keeping something and still making it yours: a seasoning, not a correction.

cocktail.closingLine: Shake it hard, keep it sharp, and serve it to whoever rolls their eyes.
cocktail.glassware: a saucer coupe (a wide, shallow stemmed glass), chilled
method: Put the glass in the freezer for ten minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you make the drink and tip that out before you pour.
Drop three basil leaves into the shaker. Add the vodka, orange liqueur, lime juice and cranberry.
Fill the shaker with ice, close it, and shake hard for about twelve seconds, until the outside is almost too cold to hold.
Pour it into the glass through the shaker's strainer, with a small tea strainer held underneath, so no bits of basil or ice get through.
Hold the lemon peel over the drink, coloured side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the surface. Then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Still Yours

cocktail.tagline: You liked it first. You get to like it last.

reading.epigraph: It was made for the staff. It didn't stay there.
whoYouAre: You rarely set out to start anything. You just like what you like a little before everyone else does: a song, a way of dressing, a word, a place nobody goes yet. You wear it or play it or order it because it's yours. Then, a while later, you notice other people doing it too, and it honestly surprises you every time.

The part you keep to yourself comes next. Once it's everywhere, it's usually done a bit worse, and the people whose taste you respect start rolling their eyes at it. Quietly, you go off it. You've let go of things you loved just because too many people started loving them. Nobody gets to tell you what to like. That includes telling you to stop. And without meaning to, you hand people something they rarely name: the nerve to love a thing before anyone else does.
yours: Most likely in 1988, at the Odeon, a restaurant in lower Manhattan, a bartender named Toby Cecchini heard about a drink from San Francisco called the Cosmopolitan. By his account, it was cheap vodka with bottled lime and grenadine, and he didn't think much of it. So he remade it: a lemon vodka that was new that year, fresh lime and Cointreau the way the bar made its Margaritas, and a splash of the sweetened cranberry juice the bar kept for another drink. It was for the staff.

Then customers started asking for it, which puzzled him. Other bars began making it, "wrong and badly", he says. By 1990 it was all over New York, and it became the one drink of its time that nearly everyone knew by name. The bartenders who came after turned against it, flavoured vodka, processed cranberry and all. Young ones would give him grief for it, and he'd apologise. For years he played it down. In 2014 he said that five years earlier he'd have asked to be "unshackled" from it.

Then that changed. Last I read, in 2026, he still makes it at his own bar in Brooklyn, and he likes it, in his word, "shrill". I like to think he found out what you keep finding out: going off something because of who else has it is just another way of letting them choose for you.

He fixed it mostly with what was already behind the bar. The cocktail I've made for you keeps his proportions, two parts lemon vodka to one each of orange liqueur, fresh lime and sweetened cranberry, and takes one thing from the kitchen: three basil leaves, shaken with it and strained out, leaving their scent and a little of their taste. They add nothing he'd measure: no sugar, no sharpness, no strength. That part is for you. Basil and cranberry are an unexpected match, and basil and lime are old friends. It goes into a wide, shallow glass, with his lemon peel squeezed over the top.

The next time something of yours turns up everywhere, and the eye-rolling starts, don't quietly let it go. Wear it, play it, order it anyway, out loud. You never gave something up because everyone else did. Don't give it up because everyone else found it.
